html:
A vast network of earth walls and ditches around Benin City and the farmland of the kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria. Built over several centuries, they are among the largest earthworks ever made.

The walls are called iya by the Edo people. Each was made by digging a deep ditch and piling the earth into a bank beside it. Around the city itself, the inner moat and wall formed a strong defence, and tradition credits the obas Oguola and Ewuare with building or enlarging them. Across the countryside, hundreds of other walls enclosed villages and their fields.

The British archaeologist Patrick Darling surveyed them in the 1990s and estimated a combined length of around 16,000 kilometres. Much of the work may date from about 800 to 1400, before the great age of the Benin obas.

Many walls were damaged after the British attack of 1897, when the city was burned and the Benin Bronzes were looted. A similar earthwork, Sungbo's Eredo, lies in Yoruba country to the west.
sum: A vast network of earth walls and ditches around Benin City and the farmland of the kingdom of Benin, in what is now southern Nigeria. Built over several centuries, they are among the largest earthworks ever made.
